articles.text: The article in the last Cow Boy and the petition relative to the organization of the county seems to have stirred up considerable feeling among the cattle men. A review of the whole case may explain matters. Two or three years ago a petition was circulated by the cattle men for the organization of the county. In answer to this petition, commissioners were appointed, Messrs. Fisher, of Medora; Hay, of Belfield, and Doyle of Bismarck. This was under the Ordway regime, and as Doyle never had, as near as we can learn, been inside of Billings county, there was another hitch in the proceedings. During a recent visit to Bismarck, the governor, whose every act since coming to Dakota has been for the best interest of Dakotains, spoke to us relative to the organization of the county. We explained that the cattle men desired more than anything else, the repeal of the herd law, and that they had already petitioned for the organization of the county as the first step toward that end. The governor then said that he had examined all the papers left by his predecessor in office, and that there was no petition on file for the organization of the county, and that there was nowhere a record of it. That he had no official knowledge of any such petition, and, as he would like to have the matter settled, asked us to take it in hand to circulate one. To this we readily acceded, and in last week's Cow Boy published a notice to the effect that such a petition was here awaiting signatures. Several came to the office and signed it, and upon its presentation to some cattle men, they absolutely refused. As the petition was directly in the interests of the cattle men, we confess this rather put a damper to it, and as it was a matter of little moment to us, except indirectly toward the development of the county, we dropped the matter. The cattle men at some time will realize their mistake, as the herd law cannot be repealed unless the county is organized, and the expenses this law entails upon the stock grower are far greater than those of a county organization.
articles.summary: Packard explains the history of the Billings County organization petition, the governor's request that he circulate a new one, and why he dropped it after cattlemen refused to sign.

articles.headline: School Meeting.
articles.text:
As per announcement in the Cow Boy, a meeting was held in Roberts' hall last Saturday evening for the purpose of organizing a school board. The meeting was called to order by M. M. Coleman, who nominated J. C. Fisher for chairman. Carried.

John S. Warn nominated L. C. Luke for secretary. Carried.

Comments were then made by several as to the object of the meeting. The chair decided that the election of a school board was in order.

On motion of M. M. Coleman, J. C. Fisher was elected secretary of the board to serve also as director. Carried.

Howard Eaton moved that E. G. Paddock be elected a member of the board. Carried.

M. M. Coleman moved that James Hannigan be elected as president of the board. Carried.

A. T. Packard moved that Wm. Van Driesche be elected treasurer of the board. Carried.

A. T. Packard moved that the school board have complete authority in the premises and be empowered to transact all school business that shall arise. Carried.

The Marquise offered the church for a school house. Referred to school board. Adjourned.
articles.summary: Minutes of the meeting in Roberts' hall that organized Medora's first school board.

articles.headline: Additional Local.
articles.text: C. W. Sleeper returned last night from his trip to the Hills. Like every one else he was astonished with the progress made by the Hillers, and is a firm believer in their future.
articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper returns from the Black Hills.

articles.text: Father Martin held mass here Tuesday morning, and during the rest of the day circulated a petition for establishing a library. The books will be here in about a week, and John O'Sullivan will act as librarian.
articles.summary: Father Martin says mass and circulates a petition for a Medora library, with John O'Sullivan as librarian.

articles.text: The new slaughter and cold storage houses of the N. P. R. C. Co., being so near completion call for a more extended mention. The main refrigerator building is 40x120 feet, and 28 feet high. The slaughter house proper is 60x105 feet. Besides these there will be a corridor 25x120 feet, and a passage way 15x80 feet. All these buildings except the ice house will have gravel roofs. This will be shingled. The foreman of the carpenter crew is John McGee, and L. Ayers is superintending in the interest of the N. P. R. R. The buildings are said to be the strongest ever built in the territory, and a glance at the immense timbers that have gone into the work will easily convince any one of this fact. Mr. McGee is pushing the work rapidly, and it will be completed in a few weeks. The N. P. R. C. Co. will be in a position to handle almost any number of cattle when the killing season again opens. It is the present expectation that three hundred will be a small day's killing. Enough workmen will be employed to make a small town of themselves, and when the spring season begins, this, in addition to other interests, will cause Medora to have an even greater proportional growth than we have had this year.
articles.summary: Description of the nearly finished N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. slaughter and cold-storage buildings at Medora.

articles.headline: Notice.
articles.text:
To prevent bulls running on the range during the winter, for the benefit of cattle men, I have established and fitted up a bull ranch on the Little Missouri. I will receive, care for and feed hay to all bulls given in my charge for the sum of $2 per month per bull. The bull round-up started on Monday, November 18th, 1884, and all bulls will be received at the Royal Chambord ranch.

For further particulars apply to Pierre Wibaux, Royal Chambord ranch. Postoffice address, Minguseville, Dawson county, Dakota.

Pierre Wibaux.
articles.summary: Pierre Wibaux announces a winter bull ranch at his Royal Chambord ranch, boarding bulls at $2 a month.

articles.headline: Strayed.
articles.text:
From North Grand river, near stage station on November 3d, a light bay horse, five years old, about 16 hands high weighs about 1,300. Has a scar on the fleshy part of the left thigh, just below the tail, one white hind foot; on each front leg just above the fetlock joint has a small knot or splint, and shoulder badly galled with some white hairs on shoulder. Also a brown horse branded U S on left shoulder, I C on left side of hip and neck., is pigeon-toed in left fore foot. About ten years old weighs about 1,000 pounds. A reward of twenty dollars ($20) will be paid for information leading to their recovery.

Wm. Miller, Minnesela, Butte Co., Dak.
articles.summary: Wm. Miller of Minnesela offers $20 for two horses strayed from the North Grand river stage station on Nov. 3.

articles.headline: NOTICE. Of a Proposed Meeting of the Stockmen of the Little Missouri.
articles.text:
At the request of Messrs. Huidekooper, Wadsworth, Eaton, Truscott, the N. P. R. C. Co. and of several other stockmen having ranges on the Little Missouri and Beaver Creek, a meeting of the stockmen of this river and its tributaries is hereby called to be held in Roberts Hall, Medora at 11 a. m. Friday December 19th. The object is to bring together the cattlemen of this vicinity in order that they may discuss certain questions of immediate and pressing interest to them, and in order that they may take measures to provide for a more efficient organization of the stockmen of this vicinity in the future, both so that they may be able to act more as a unit than has been the case in the past, and so that they can combine to protect their interests against unjust interference from the outside.

All gentlemen interested in stock raising both those on the Little Missouri, and those on the neighboring waters, are urgently requested to attend.

[By request.]

Theodore Roosevelt.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt, at the request of leading ranchers, calls a meeting of Little Missouri stockmen at Roberts Hall, Medora, on Friday, December 19.

articles.text: The recent stock meeting at St. Louis probably destined to have great weight on the future of stock growing in the west. Not much real business was transacted, but the foundations were laid for years of it. The subject of a national trail was the principal topic discussed, and a committee was appointed to memorialize congress in its favor. Colorado and Texas combined against the other states and territories, and finally downed them on the chairmanship, J. L. Routt[?] being elected. An association was organized under the name of the National Live Stock Association of America, and a constitution was adopted. The subject of cattle contagion caused extended remarks, and considerable feeling was aroused at the efforts of specialists to magnify the disease and thus place themselves prominently before the public. The subject of the dreadful scourge made by the drouth in Virginia and West Virginia, came to the attention of the meeting and in a few moments $1,200 was raised and telegraphed to the sufferers. The question of leasing public lands to cattle growers so that they might have a certainty of a possessory right for a time at least called for the greatest display of oratory during the convention. It was finally voted that it would be better to lease the lands, as at present no cattle man feels like making any improvements when he is liable at any time to be dispossessed by a homesteader. The president for the ensuing year is Col. R. D. Hunter of St. Louis. The next place for holding the annual meeting was decided by the executive committee to be St. Louis.
articles.summary: Report on the St. Louis cattle convention: national trail, the new National Live Stock Association, contagion, and leasing public lands.

articles.text: Of all the finer cattle imported into Colorado the present season, the Shorthorns had the majority. The importations consisted of high grade bulls under two years of age. In Wyoming the Herefords were slightly in the lead. But be it said that those taken in there had a mixture of the Shorthorn with the Hereford blood. The popular cross in that grazing country is a whiteface mixed on a Durham. The largest number of imported cattle that came into Colorado, were Galloways and Polled-Angus.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipping on breeds of cattle imported into Colorado and Wyoming; the paper printed this item twice in column 7.

articles.text: The Oregon Horse and Land company, whose ranch is on Snake river, in Oregon, has the largest horse outfit in the United States, 7,200 head running on the range. The company has shipped this season 500 head of geldings to the eastern markets, one firm in New York taking 200 head, and the street car company of Chicago took five car loads at an average price of $127 per head, unbroken. The manager says the difference in price between broken and unbroken horses is too small to pay for the trouble of training.—[Stock Growers' Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping on the Oregon Horse and Land Company's horse herd.

articles.text: It is claimed by some of the Texas drovers that the day for big herds on the trail is over, and that cattle from that state will mostly come to market by rail. If such should be the case, much of western life would be done away with. What would the annual shipment be to the cowboy without life on the trail? Going up the trail in the spring has long been a looked for job by the cowboy, and one which has afforded him a change from every day life on the ranch, which combined pleasure with their business. Viewing it other than from a business stand point we would miss the annual visit of the great herds and their drivers.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipping lamenting the possible end of the Texas trail drives.

articles.text: The sporting season of 1884 is over, and the records now made are not liable to be changed before the return of the warm months. Maud S., though unsuccessful in beating her own 2.09¾, remains Queen of the trotting turf, with the little gelding Jay-Eye-See a close second for first honors. Johnston (2.06¼), the fastest living horse outside of the thoroughbreds, leads both and so widens the gap between pacing and trotting as to render it somewhat doubtful as to whether it will ever be closed. Over this problem, and the other which the past season has furnished, horsemen can ponder without interruption in the succeeding six months.—[Pittsburgh Stockman.
articles.summary: Clipping on the 1884 harness-racing records.

articles.text: Texas has produced three hundred thousand calves the present year that will be looking for a market as yearlings early next spring. "What we are to do with them yearlings is what immediately concerns us," remarks the Stockman, of San Antonio. That there will be as great a demand for them in this north country as there was the present year is quite uncertain. The men who bought young cattle this year paid too high a price for them, and if a hard winter should follow, will surely lose money. It will be somewhat doubtful, too, if many are brought by rail next season, as the territories and some of the States will quarantine against their coming in that way on account of the fever scare charged to that mode of transportation; and the driving across the Indian country and through a corner of Kansas will be attended with much trouble from the Indians and the white settlers. And if the Government refuses to open a national trail up from that country to the northwest it will still be worse with the calf growers in the south in the years to come. We believe it is to the interest of Colorado that facilities be afforded and maintained for the moving of the young herds of bovines as they come along from that country to this. Here is the proper feeding ground, there the breeding. Ninety-five per cent. of the cows of Texas will drop calves and raise them, while in Colorado not more than sixty will do it.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipping on the market for Texas yearlings and the need for a national cattle trail.

articles.text: At Medora, George Heywood entered Robert's saloon armed for the purpose of killing him, and in attempting to shoot was suddenly stopped by Roberts drawing a revolver and firing, the ball taking effect in Heywood's left breast. The wound is not considered dangerous.
articles.summary: Syndicated Dakota Territorial News item (ready-print page) reporting that saloon keeper Roberts shot George Heywood, who had come to kill him.

articles.text: Cigars and tobacco at Cook's.
articles.summary: Advertising local for Cook's store.

articles.text: Dr. Heber Robarts, of Dickinson, is a frequent visitor to Medora.
articles.summary: Dr. Heber Robarts of Dickinson visits Medora often.

articles.text: The Marquise de Mores left for St. Paul and New York yesterday morning. She does not expect to return until spring.
articles.summary: The Marquise de Mores leaves for St. Paul and New York for the winter.

articles.text: M. Coleman has made a number of improvements on his hotel, and now says that with the assistance of the coal mine he is prepared for any weather that may turn up.
articles.summary: Coleman improves the Medora Hotel for winter.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts sold his tame buffalo to Bob. Roberts, who shipped it to Bismarck Monday. It will there be killed, stuffed and sent to New Orleans. Bob. sent the pet bear in the same car to Bismarck as a present to George Reed.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts's tame buffalo is shipped to Bismarck to be stuffed for New Orleans, with a pet bear sent to George Reed.

articles.text: S. Jacques, representing the Illustrated Northwest, was here yesterday in its interest. The Northwest has probably done more than any other publication toward developing our country, and Mr. Jacques is an able exponent of its virtues.
articles.summary: S. Jacques of the Illustrated Northwest visits Medora.

articles.text: Count Rembielinski of Russia and Vic. Smith have been hunting down the river for about ten days, and during that time, the Count killed sixty-five deer and antelope. This is the best tenderfoot record to date. Vic. says he is a dandy.
articles.summary: Count Rembielinski and guide Vic. Smith hunt down the river; the Count kills sixty-five deer and antelope.

articles.text: [B. Rumsey?], who has been here for some time, recently bought twenty-eight Durham bulls of the N. P. R. C. Co. They were branded Tuesday in the stable corrall, and the boys showed wonderful agility in climbing fences when they were turned loose.
articles.summary: A Medora rancher buys twenty-eight Durham bulls from the N. P. R. C. Co.; they are branded Tuesday.

articles.text: George Fitzgerald is going to work in earnest on his new hotel, and expects to have it finished, with the possible exception of the brick work, by January 15. We have seen the plans, and they show that it will be a first-class building. Peter Book has the whole contract.
articles.summary: George Fitzgerald's new hotel, built by Peter Book, is to be finished by January 15.

articles.text: Mr. Simpson of St. Paul arrived Sunday evening and began his duties immediately as traffic manager of the stage company. Such an office has been badly needed, both in seeing that shipping directions are complied with and in getting additional freight, express and passengers.
articles.summary: Mr. Simpson of St. Paul arrives to become traffic manager of the stage company.

articles.text: The secretary of the school board left before handing us the minutes of the board meeting. We learn, however, that the position of teacher was offered to Mrs. Barr, who was obliged to refuse on account of a trip east, and that it was decided to hold the school for a time, at least, at the cantonment.
articles.summary: The school board offers the teaching post to Mrs. Barr, who declines; school is to be held at the cantonment.

articles.text: At a recent meeting the stage company was reorganized with the following result; Marquis de Mores, president and general manager; F. B. Allen, vice-president; A. T. Packard, secretary; William VanDriesche, treasurer; A. N. Simpson, traffic manager; J. C. Fisher, auditor, and E. Deffebach, superintendent.
articles.summary: The stage company reorganizes with the Marquis de Mores as president and general manager and Packard as secretary.

articles.text: Otto Fischer, of Bismarck, arrived yesterday morning, and proceeded to make it lively for the boys. As may be seen by the advertisement, he is manager of the Bismarck branch of the Franz Falk Brewing Co., of which Roberts & Co. are local agents. Where Otto can't drum up trade, others had better not try.
articles.summary: Otto Fischer of the Franz Falk Brewing Co.'s Bismarck branch visits Medora.

articles.text: The weather report handed us by T. Martin is a sufficient evidence of the superiority of our climate. Mr. Martin has kept the weather record for years in the Hills, and says he has never seen anywhere near as good weather for this season. His reports will be published monthly hereafter, and will be eagerly awaited.
articles.summary: T. Martin's weather reports will appear monthly.

articles.text: F. B. Allen, of Bismarck, came down Saturday night. As Luke would say, "He had the veneered gall to wear a plug." The boys seemed to think that the plug had a tendency to make Allen's head bald or something, and their intention was the best in the world to give it plenty of ventilation. F. B. was too cute, however, as the plug didn't show up until he was starting away.
articles.summary: F. B. Allen of Bismarck visits Medora wearing a plug hat.

articles.text: A correspondent writes that: "Hunters should always carry a watch or clock. That is what Tom Caruthers says and believes. L. Austin Paddock and Amos Stowe of Wadena, Minn., came here a short time ago to paint the buttes with gore. They went down the river with Tom Caruthers. Austin, who was panting too hard for game to sleep, roused up the boys at 2 a. m. They laid in some grub and then took a sleep. Austin meantime aimed his gun at the fire, and thought he could just knock the eye out of a fawn every time at one hundred yards. After fondling his gun for a few hours, Austin roused the boys a a second time and cooked a second breakfast. This suited the boys pretty well, and they took another sleep. Austin was just getting breakfast for the third time, when Tom made a break for the bullberry bushes and hid till Austin left camp. Tom says he is not stuck on night hunting, and will take a rest while Austin is here."
articles.summary: Humorous correspondent's account of L. Austin Paddock and Amos Stowe of Wadena, Minn., hunting with Tom Caruthers.

articles.headline: Fitting Thanks.
articles.text:
Several of our Catholic citizens, desiring to express their sense of obligation to the Marquise de Mores, have signed the following. It would only have been a matter of time to get the signatures of all, both Catholic and Protestant, as the church is a great improvement to our town:

We, the undersigned Catholics of Medora and Little Missouri, wish to express our thanks in this public manner to the Marquise de Mores for her kindness in building and donating the church to us.

Martin Timlin,
M. T. Smith,
John O'Sullivan,
C. Gallagher,
M. M. Coleman,
Patrick O'Hara.

Confectionery of all kinds at Cook's.
articles.summary: Catholics of Medora and Little Missouri publicly thank the Marquise de Mores for building and donating their church.
